translations.text: After Joshua died, the Israelites asked the Lord, saying, “Who will go up first for us against the Canaanites to fight them?”
The Lord said, “Judah will go up, for I have given the land into his hands.”
Judah said to his brother Simeon, “Go up with me into my allotted territory, and let us fight the Canaanites. Then I too will go with you into your allotted territory.” So Simeon went with him.
Judah went up, and the Lord gave the Canaanites and the Perizzites into his hands. He struck down ten thousand of their men at Bezek.
They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek, fought against him, and struck down the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and big toes.

Adoni-bezek said, “Seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off used to gather crumbs beneath my table. Now God has repaid me just as I did to them.” They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.
The people of Judah fought against Jerusalem, captured it, struck it with the edge of the sword, and burned the city with fire.
After that, the people of Judah went down to fight the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, in the south, and in the plains.

Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron, and Hebron came out against him. Hebron had formerly been named Kiriath-arba Sepher. They struck down Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak.
From there they went up against the inhabitants of Debir. Debir had formerly been named the City of Letters.
Caleb said, “Whoever attacks the City of Letters and captures it, I will give him my daughter Achsah as his wife.”
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s brother, who was younger than he was, captured it, and Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as his wife.

As she was going, Othniel urged her to ask her father for a field. She complained and cried out from the donkey, saying, “You have given me land in the south.” Caleb said to her, “What is the matter with you?”
Achsah said to him, “Give me a blessing. Since you have given me land in the south, give me pools of water as well.” Caleb gave her the upper pools and the pools in the valleys, as she desired.

The descendants of Hobab the Kenite, Moses’ father-in-law, went up from the City of Palms with the people of Judah into the wilderness of Judah, which is south of Judah, near the slope of Arad. They went and settled among the people.
Judah went with his brother Simeon, and they struck down the Canaanites who lived in Zephath. They placed it under a curse and destroyed it, and they named the city Destruction.
Judah did not take possession of Gaza and its territory, Ashkelon and its territory, Ekron and its territory, or Ashdod and its fields.
The Lord was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country. But they could not dispossess the inhabitants of the valleys, because Rechab separated them, and they had iron chariots.
They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said. He took possession of the three cities of the sons of Anak there and removed the thirty sons of Anak from there.
The people of Benjamin did not dispossess the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem. The Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.
The descendants of Joseph also went up to Bethel, and the Lord was with them.
The house of Israel camped at Bethel. The city had formerly been named Luz.
The guards saw a man coming out of the city. They seized him and said, “Show us the entrance to this city, and we will show you mercy.”
He showed them the entrance to the city, and they struck the city with the edge of the sword. But they let the man and his family go.
The man went to the land of the Hittites, built a city there, and named it Luz. That is its name to this day.

Manasseh did not take possession of Beth-shean, which is Scythopolis, or its dependent towns or its fields, or Taanach and its dependent towns, or the inhabitants of Dor, those living around it, and its dependent towns, or the inhabitants of Balak, those living around it, and its dependent towns, or the inhabitants of Ibleam, those living around it, and its dependent towns. The Canaanites began to dwell in that land.
When Israel grew strong, they subjected the Canaanites to tribute, but did not drive them out completely.
Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer. The Canaanites lived among them in Gezer and became subject to tribute.
Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kedron or the inhabitants of Aman. The Canaanites lived among them and became subject to tribute.
Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, who became subject to tribute, or the inhabitants of Dor, Sidon, and Ahlab, or those of Achzib, Elpha, Aphek, and Rehob.
Asher lived among the Canaanites who inhabited the land, because they could not drive them out.

Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh or the inhabitants of Beth-anath. Naphtali lived among the Canaanites who inhabited the land, and the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath became subject to tribute.
The Amorites confined the descendants of Dan to the mountain, because they would not allow them to go down into the valleys.

The Amorites began to live on the mountain of the myrtle grove, where there were bears and foxes, in the myrtle groves and in Shaalbim. Joseph’s hand grew strong against the Amorites, and they became subject to tribute.
For the boundary of the Amorites, the Edomites, was above the slope of Akrabbim, from the rock upward.

The angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to the place of weeping, to Bethel, and to the house of Israel, and said to them, “Thus says the Lord: The Lord brought you up from Egypt and brought you into this land, which he swore to your ancestors to give you. And he says to you, ‘I will never break my covenant with you.’”

“Do not make a covenant with the inhabitants of this land or with their gods, and do not worship them. Instead, smash their carved images and tear down their altars. But you did not obey my voice. Why have you done this?”

“And I said, ‘I will no longer displace the people whom I continued to destroy, nor will I drive them out before you. They will become a danger to you, and their gods will become a stumbling block to you.’”
When the angel of the Lord spoke these words to all the descendants of Israel, the people raised their voices and wept.
For this reason, that place was named Weeping, and they offered sacrifices there to the Lord.
Joshua dismissed the people, and the descendants of Israel went, each to his own home and his own inheritance, to take possession of the land.
The people served the Lord throughout Joshua’s lifetime and throughout the lifetime of the elders who outlived Joshua and who knew all the great deeds that the Lord had done in Israel.
Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of one hundred and ten.
They buried him on the mountain of his inheritance, at Timnath-heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
That entire generation was gathered to their ancestors. Another generation arose after them who did not know the Lord or the deeds he had done among Israel.
The descendants of Israel did evil in the Lord’s sight and worshiped the Baals.

They abandoned the Lord, the God of their ancestors, who had brought them out of the land of the Egyptians. They followed foreign gods, the gods of the nations around them, and bowed down to them, provoking the Lord to anger.
They abandoned him and worshiped Baal and the Astartes.

The Lord’s anger burned against Israel. The Lord handed them over to plunderers, who ravaged them, and the Lord handed them over to their enemies all around. They could not stand against any of their enemies, with whom they had prostituted themselves.
The Lord’s hand was against them for harm, just as the Lord had said and just as the Lord had sworn, and he afflicted them severely.
The Lord raised up judges for them, and the Lord rescued them from the hands of those who plundered them.

Yet they did not listen to them either, but prostituted themselves by following foreign gods and bowed down to them. They provoked the Lord to anger and quickly turned aside from the path their fathers had followed in obeying the Lord’s commandments. They did not do as their fathers had done.

Whenever the Lord raised up judges for them, the Lord was with the judge and saved them from the hands of their enemies throughout the judge’s lifetime. For the Lord relented because of their groaning under those who besieged and oppressed them.

But whenever the judge died, they turned back and became more corrupt than their fathers, following foreign gods, serving them, and bowing down to them. They did not abandon their practices or turn away from their stubborn ways.
The Lord became fiercely angry with Israel and said, “Because this nation has abandoned my covenant, which I commanded their fathers to keep, and has not obeyed my voice,
I too will no longer drive out anyone before them from the nations that Joshua son of Nun left behind.”
He left them to test Israel through them, to see whether they would take care to walk in the Lord’s way, as their fathers had taken care to do, or not.
So the Lord left those nations, not driving them out quickly, and did not deliver them into Joshua’s hands.
These are the nations that Joshua left to test through them all those in Israel who had not known any of the wars with the Canaanites,
but only so that the generations of the Israelites might be taught warfare; those who came before them had not known it either:
the five lordships of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon to Lebo-hamath.
They were there to test Israel through them, to find out whether they would obey the Lord’s commandments, which he had given their fathers through Moses.
The Israelites lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites, and Girgashites.
They took their daughters as wives for themselves and gave their own daughters to their sons, and they served their gods.
The Israelites did evil in the Lord’s sight, forgot the Lord their God, and served Baal and the sacred groves.
The Lord became fiercely angry with Israel and delivered them into the hands of Cushan-rishathaim, king of the Syrians of Mesopotamia. They served him for eight years.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up a deliverer for Israel. He gave them Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s brother, who was younger than Caleb, and he heard them.

The Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war against Cushan-rishathaim, and the Lord delivered Cushan-rishathaim, king of the Syrians, into his hands. His hand prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim.
The land had rest for forty years, and Othniel son of Kenaz died.
The Israelites again did evil in the Lord’s sight, and the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against Israel because they had done evil in the Lord’s sight.
He gathered all the Ammonites and Amalek against them, went and defeated Israel, and took possession of the City of Palms.
The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years.

The Israelites cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up a deliverer for them: Ehud son of Gera, the son of a Benjaminite man, who was skilled with both hands. The Israelites sent tribute through him to Eglon king of Moab.
Ehud made himself a double-edged sword a span long, fastened it to his right thigh under his cloak, and went.
He presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Eglon was a very fat man.
When Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away those who had carried it.

And Eglon returned from the carved images, together with Gilgal, and Ehud said, “I have something to tell you in secret, O king.” Eglon said, “Be silent.” And he said to everyone, “Go away.” Those who stood beside him went outside.
He was sitting alone in his cool upper room, and Ehud said, “I have a message from God for you, O king.” Eglon rose from his seat and approached him.
As he rose, Ehud stretched out his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and struck Eglon in the side.
He pushed the hilt in after the blade, and the fat closed over the opening of the wound, because he did not pull the sword out of his side.
He went out onto the porch, passed through the latticework, closed the doors of the upper room behind him, and bolted them.
He himself went out and left. His servants came in and saw that the doors of the upper room were locked, and they said, “Perhaps he is sitting on the seat, relieving himself in the chamber.”
They stood waiting until they were embarrassed, but no one opened the doors of the upper room. They took the key and opened them, and there was their master, lying dead on the ground.
Ehud escaped to Seirah while they were in confusion, and no one paid attention to him. He passed by the carved images and escaped, reaching Seirah.
When Ehud came into the land of Israel, he blew a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites came down with him from the hills, and he went before them.

He said to them, “Come down after me, for the Lord our God has delivered our enemies, the Moabites, into our hands.” They came down after him and first seized the Jordan crossings leading to Moab, and they allowed no one to cross.
That day they struck down about ten thousand men of Moab—all their fighting men and every mighty warrior. Not a single man survived.
Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel, and the land had rest for eighty years. Ehud judged them until he died.

After him arose Shamgar son of Anath. He struck down six hundred Philistine men with the handle of a plow and took as spoil very many cattle and sheep, not counting the calves of the cattle. He saved Israel.
The Israelites again did evil before the Lord, and Shamgar died.
The Lord delivered them into the hands of Jabin, king of the Canaanites, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of their army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth of the Nations.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord, because Jabin had nine hundred iron chariots, and he severely oppressed Israel for twenty years.
Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time.
She lived beneath the palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites went up to her for judgment.

Deborah sent and summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali, and said to him, “Has not the Lord, the God of Israel, commanded you: ‘Go to Mount Tabor and take with you ten thousand men from the descendants of Naphtali and the descendants of Zebulun,
and bring them with you to the Kishon ravine against Sisera, the commander of Jabin’s army, and against his troops and his chariots? I will deliver him into your hands.’”
Barak said to her, “If you go with me, I will go; but if you do not go with me, I will not go, because I do not know the day on which the Lord will grant success to his angel accompanying me.”

Deborah said to him, “I will certainly go with you, but know that the honor will not be yours on the journey you are taking, for the Lord will deliver Sisera into the hands of a woman.” Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh.
Barak gave orders to Zebulun and Naphtali at Kedesh, and ten thousand men went up after him. Deborah also went up with him.
The relatives of the Kenite separated from the Kenites, from the descendants of Hobab, Moses’ father-in-law, and he pitched his tent beside the oak of those at rest, which is near Kedesh.
Sisera was informed that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor.
Sisera gathered all his chariots, nine hundred iron chariots, and all the troops with him, from Harosheth of the nations to the Kishon torrent.

Deborah said to Barak, “Rise, for this is the day on which the Lord has delivered Sisera into your hands. Look, the Lord is ahead of you!” Barak came down from Mount Tabor, with ten thousand men following him.
The Lord threw Sisera, all his chariots, and his entire army into panic before Barak at the edge of the sword. Sisera got down from his chariot and fled on foot.
Barak pursued the chariots and the army as far as the forest of the nations. Sisera’s entire army fell by the edge of the sword; not even one remained.
Sisera went away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the household of Heber the Kenite.
Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, “Turn aside to me, my lord, turn aside, and do not be afraid.” He turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with its flaps.
Sisera said to her, “Give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty.” She opened the skin of milk, gave him a drink, and covered his face.
Sisera said to her, “Stand at the entrance of your tent. If anyone comes to you and asks, ‘Is there a man here?’ say, ‘No.’”

She covered him beneath her tent flaps. Then Jael, Heber’s wife, took a tent peg and held a hammer in her hand. She went quietly up to him, drove the peg through his temple, and fastened it into the ground. He fell between her feet and breathed his last.

Now Barak was coming in determined pursuit of Sisera. Jael went out to meet him and said, “Come here, and I will show you the man you are looking for.” He went in with her, and there lay Sisera, fallen dead, with the peg in his temple.
On that day the Lord God brought Jabin king of the Canaanites low before the Israelites.
The Israelites’ power grew increasingly strong against Jabin king of the Canaanites, until they destroyed them.
On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang praises, saying:
When Israel’s commanders took the lead and the people acted willingly, bless the Lord!
Hear, kings, and listen, rulers! I will sing to the Lord and sing psalms to the God of Israel.
Lord, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the fields of Edom, the earth shook, the heavens were stirred, and the clouds dripped water.
The mountains shook before the Lord [?] of Sinai, before the Lord, the God of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, kings were no more, and those who traveled along paths went along winding roads.
Village dwellers disappeared from Israel; they disappeared until Deborah arose, until a mother arose in Israel.
They desired foreign, worthless gods as they would a barley cake. Then the cities of rulers went to war under the protection of new spears—forty thousand men in Israel.
My heart is with Israel’s appointed leaders. You mighty men of the people, bless the Lord!
You who ride horses at midday and white [?], who go to the courts of judges,

Raise your voices with the sound of musicians among those who rejoice. There they will proclaim the Lord’s righteousness; he displayed righteousness among Israel. Then the Lord’s people came down into the cities.
Awake, awake, Deborah! Rouse the tens of thousands together with the people! Awake, awake! Speak in songs! Rise up in strength, Barak! Take your captives captive, son of Abinoam!
Then his strength increased. The Lord drove back for me those stronger than I.

The people of Ephraim punished them in the valleys; your brother Benjamin, your own people. From me, from Machir, scouts came down, and from Zebulun, those who give strength with the staff of the scribe’s account.
The commanders of Issachar were with Deborah and with Barak, and then Barak stretched out his feet into the valleys. Among the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.
Why should they sit in the midst of Mosphathema, listening to the cries of those in distress, to pass into Reuben’s territory? Great searches of heart have arisen.
Gad settled beyond the Jordan. And Dan, why do you remain abroad in ships? Asher settled along the seashore and will dwell in its inlets.
Zebulun is a people who despised their own lives even to death, and Naphtali was on the heights of the open country.
Kings came and fought; then the kings of the Canaanites were hard pressed at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo. I took no silver as plunder.
The stars fought from heaven; from their respective stations they waged war against Sisera.
The torrent of Kishon swept them away, the torrent of Kadesim, the torrent of Kishon. My soul will trample them; my feet will be strengthened with might.
Then the horses’ heels were shattered at Maddaroth, and my heels will trample the arrogance of their terrors.
“Curse Meroz,” says the angel of the Lord. “Utterly curse its inhabitants, because they did not come to help the Lord.” The Lord, the Mighty One, is a helper among the warriors.
Blessed among women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite; blessed among women be she in her tent.
He asked for water, and she gave him milk; in a bowl fit for the mighty she offered curds.

She stretched out her left hand toward the tent peg and her right hand for utterly crushing blows, to disable him. She brought Sisera to his end, drove it through his jaws, passed the peg through his head, and killed him.
Between her feet he fell, overcome, and she put him to sleep between her knees. Where he bent down until he was laid low, there the wretched man fell.

Sisera’s mother looked out and kept watch through the latticed window, for she saw those returning from Sisera. “Why are his chariots late in coming? Why have the tracks of his chariots been delayed?”
The wise women of his princes answered her in reply and spoke, and she herself also gave herself an answer:

“Will not the dividers of the spoil find him, making love to companions for each man? And [?] his entrails. Spoils of dyed cloth for Sisera, spoils of dyed cloth with multicolored designs, a band with varied designs—that was the spoil for his neck.”
So may all your enemies perish, Lord, and may those who love him be like the sun rising in its strength.
And the land had rest for forty years.
The Israelites did evil before the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years.
The hand of Midian grew strong against Israel, and because of Midian the Israelites made shelters for themselves in the mountains, in caves, and in strongholds.
Whenever an Israelite plowed, Midian, Amalek, and the people of the east would come up against them.
They camped beside them and destroyed the produce of the land as far as the approaches to Gaza. They left Israel no means of subsistence, neither sheep nor cattle nor donkeys.
For they came up with their livestock and brought their tents. They arrived as numerous as locusts; neither they nor their camels could be counted. They came into the land of Israel to destroy it.
Israel became very poor because of Midian, and the Israelites cried out to the Lord.
And when the Israelites cried out to the Lord because of Midian,

the Lord sent a prophet to the Israelites, and he said to them, “Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: I am the one who brought you up from the land of the Egyptians and rescued you from the house of slavery.
I delivered you from the hands of the Egyptians and from the hands of all your oppressors. I drove them out before you and gave you their land.
And I said to you, ‘I am the Lord your God. Do not fear the gods of the Amorites, among whom you are living in their land.’ But you did not listen to my voice.”
The angel of the Lord came and sat beneath the oak at Ophrah, belonging to Joash, the father of Esrea. Gideon his son was threshing wheat on the threshing floor to hide from Midian.
The angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, “The Lord is with you, mighty warrior.”

Gideon said to him, “Please, my lord, if the Lord was with us, why have all these evils overtaken us? Where are all his wonders that our fathers told us about, saying, ‘Did not the Lord bring us out of Egypt?’ And now why has he rejected us and handed us over to Midian?”
The angel of the Lord looked at him and said, “Go in this strength of yours, and you will save Israel from the hand of Midian. Have I not sent you?”
Gideon said to him, “Please, my lord, how can I save Israel? Look, my clan is the lowliest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s household.”
He said to him, “The Lord is with you, and you will strike down Midian as though it were one man.”
Gideon said, “If I have found favor in your eyes, give me a sign that it is you who are speaking with me.”
“Do not leave here until I come back to you, bring my offering, and set it before you.” He said, “I am, and I will stay here until you return to me.”

Gideon went inside and prepared a young goat and unleavened bread from an artaba of flour. He put the meat on a platter and poured the broth into a pot. He brought them out to him beneath the oak and bowed to the ground.
The angel of the Lord said to him, “Take the meat and the unleavened bread, put them on that rock, and pour out the broth.” And he did so.

The angel of the Lord extended the tip of the staff in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread. Fire flared up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread, and the angel of the Lord disappeared from his sight.
Gideon realized that he was the angel of the Lord, and Gideon said, “Alas, Lord, Lord! I have seen the angel of the Lord face to face!”
The Lord said to him, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid; you will not die.”
Gideon built an altar to the Lord there and called it “The Peace of the Lord,” to this day, while he himself was still there at Ophrah, belonging to his father Esrea.
That night the Lord said to him, “Take your father’s fattened bull and the second bull, the seven-year-old one. Tear down your father’s altar to Baal and cut down the grove beside it.”

“Build an altar to the Lord your God, who appeared to you, on the summit of Mount Manovza, at the place of battle. Take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering, using the wood of the grove that you will cut down.”

Gideon took thirteen men from among his servants and did as the Lord had told him. Because he was afraid of his father’s household and the men of the city, he did it at night rather than during the day.
The men of the city rose early in the morning, and there was the altar of Baal torn down, the grove beside it cut down, and the fattened bull offered as a burnt offering on the newly built altar.
They said to one another, “Who has done this?” They searched and investigated, and they said, “Gideon son of Joash has done this.”
The men of the city said to Joash, “Bring your son out, and let him die, because he demolished the altar of Baal and cut down the sacred grove beside it.”

Joash said to the men who had risen against him, “Will you now plead Baal’s case, or will you save him? Whoever has harmed him must die by morning. If he is a god, let him seek vengeance for himself, because they have torn down his altar.”
On that day he named him Jerubbaal, saying, “Baal’s judgment,” because he had torn down his altar.
All Midian and Amalek and all the people of the east gathered together and came and camped in the valleys of Jezreel.
The Spirit of the Lord strengthened Gideon. He blew the horn, and Abiezer raised a rallying cry behind him.
He sent messengers throughout all Manasseh and called them out, and Manasseh also followed him. He sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they came out to meet him.
Gideon said to God, “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said,
look, I am placing a wool fleece on the threshing floor. If there is rain on the fleece alone, while all the ground is dry, I will know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said.”
And it happened that way. Gideon rose early the next morning and squeezed the fleece, and enough dew came out of the fleece to fill a basin with water.

Gideon said to God, “Do not let your anger burn against me, and let me speak once more. Let me make one more test with the fleece: this time let the fleece alone be dry, and let there be rain on all the ground.”
God did so that night: the fleece alone was dry, and there was rain on all the ground.

Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, rose early with all the troops who were with him, and they camped beside the spring of Harod. The camp of Midian and Amalek was north of them, at Gabaatham, which was there in the valley.
The Lord said to Gideon, “The troops with you are too numerous for me to deliver Midian into their hands, lest Israel boast against me and say, ‘My own hand saved me.’”

The Lord said to him, “Speak in the hearing of the people and say, ‘Whoever is fainthearted, let him turn back.’” They set off from Mount Gilead, and twenty-two thousand returned from the army, while ten thousand remained.

The Lord said to Gideon, “Your troops are still too numerous. Bring them down to the water, and I will test them for you there. Whoever I tell you, ‘This one shall go with you,’ shall go with you; and whoever I tell you, ‘This one shall not go with you,’ shall not go with you.”

He brought the army down to the water, and the Lord said to Gideon, “Everyone who laps the water with his tongue like a dog, set them apart; and everyone who falls to his knees to drink, set them separately.”
The number of all those who lapped with their hands and their tongues was three hundred men. The rest of the people knelt down on their knees to drink water.
The Lord said to Gideon, “With these three hundred men who lapped the water, I will save you and deliver Midian into your hands. Let all the other people go, each man to his own place.”

They took the people's provisions in their hands, along with their ram's-horn trumpets. Gideon sent away every man of Israel, each to his own home, and kept only the three hundred men. The camp of Midian was below him in the valleys.
That night the Lord said to him, “Get up and go down quickly from here into the camp, for I have delivered it into your hands.
But if you are afraid to go down, first go down into the camp with your young servant Purah,
and listen to what they say. Then your hands will be strengthened, and you will go down into the camp.” So he went down with his young servant Purah to a section of the camp's companies of fifty.
Midian, Amalek, and all the people of the east were camped in the valleys, as numerous as locusts. Their camels were beyond counting, as numerous as the sand on the seashore.

Gideon entered, and there was a man telling his companion a dream. He said, “I had a dream: a loaf of barley bread was rolling into the camp of Midian. It came to the tent of Midian, struck it, and overturned it, and the tent fell upside down.”
His companion answered, “This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, an Israelite man. The Lord has delivered Midian and the entire camp into his hands.”

When Gideon heard the account of the dream and its interpretation, he bowed down before the Lord. He returned to the camp of Israel and said, “Get up, for the Lord has delivered the camp of Midian into our hands!”
He divided the three hundred men into three companies and put ram's-horn trumpets into everyone's hands, and torches inside jars.
He said to them, “Watch me and do as I do. I am going into the midst of the camp, and whatever I do, you must do likewise.”
“When I blow the ram’s horn, all of you who are with me must also blow your ram’s horns all around the camp and say, ‘The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!’”

Gideon and the hundred men with him came to the edge of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when the guards had only just been awakened. They blew the ram’s horns and smashed the jars they held in their hands.

The three divisions blew their ram’s horns and broke their jars. They held the torches in their left hands and the horns in their right hands to blow them, and they shouted, “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!”
Each man stood separately in his place around the camp. The whole camp ran, blew trumpets, and fled.

The three hundred ram’s horns sounded, and the Lord turned each man’s sword against his companion throughout the camp. The whole camp fled as far as Beth-shittah, and the other company as far as the slope of Abel-meholah and Tabath.
The men of Israel from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh rallied and pursued Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout the territory of Ephraim, saying, “Go down ahead of Midian and seize the water crossings as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.” All the men of Ephraim rallied and seized the water crossings as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.

They captured the two rulers of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb, and they pursued Midian. They brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon from the other side of the Jordan.
The men of Ephraim said to Gideon, “What is this you have done to us? Why did you not call us when you went to fight Midian?” They argued fiercely with him.
He said to them, “What have I done compared with you? Surely Ephraim’s gleanings are better than Abiezer’s harvest!”
“The Lord delivered the rulers of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, into your hands. What could I do compared with you?” Then their anger against him subsided when he spoke these words.
Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the three hundred men with him, exhausted and hungry.
He said to the men of Succoth, “Please give bread as food to these troops who are with me, for they are hungry, and I am pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.”
The rulers of Succoth said, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your troops?”
Gideon said, “Not so! When the Lord delivers Zebah and Zalmunna into my hands, I will tear your flesh with desert thorns and briers.”
He went up from there to Penuel and spoke to them in the same way. The men of Penuel answered him just as the men of Succoth had answered.
Gideon said to the men of Penuel, “When I return here in peace, I will tear down that tower.”
Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, with their army of about fifteen thousand men, all who remained of the entire army of the people of the east. One hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had fallen.
Gideon went up by the road of the tent dwellers, east of Nabae and opposite Nabea, and attacked the camp, for the camp was unsuspecting.
Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and they pursued them. He captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and threw their entire army into confusion.
Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle by the descent of Heres.
He captured a young man from among the men of Succoth, questioned him, and wrote down for himself the leaders of Succoth and its elders, seventy-seven men.

Gideon came to the leaders of Succoth and said to them, “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, on whose account you mocked me and said, ‘Are Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hands, that we should give bread to your exhausted men?’”
He took the leaders and elders of the city, along with thorns from the wilderness and briars, and dragged the men of Succoth over them.
He demolished the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.
He said to Zebah and Zalmunna, “Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?” They said, “They were just like you, resembling you, and you resemble them, like the appearance of a king’s sons.”
Gideon said, “They were my brothers, my mother’s sons.” He swore to them and said, “As the Lord lives, if you had kept them alive, I would not kill you.”
He said to Jether, his firstborn, “Get up and kill them.” But the young man did not draw his sword, because he was afraid, for he was still a boy.
Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Get up yourself and strike us down, for as a man is, so is his strength.” Gideon got up and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and took the necklaces from their camels’ necks.
The men of Israel said to Gideon, “Rule over us, you, your son, and your son’s son, because you have rescued us from the hands of Midian.”
Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, nor will my son rule over you. The Lord will rule over you.”
Gideon said to them, “I will make one request of you: let each man give me an earring from the plunder.” For they had gold earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.
They said, “We will certainly give them.” They spread out his garment, and each man threw onto it the gold earrings from his plunder.

The weight of the gold earrings that he requested was one thousand seven hundred shekels of gold, apart from the jingling ornaments, necklaces, headbands, purple garments, and whatever was on the kings of Midian, and apart from the gold necklaces on their camels’ necks.
Gideon made it into an ephod and set it up in his city, Ophrah. All Israel prostituted themselves by following it there, and it became a stumbling block to Gideon and his household.
Midian was driven back before the Israelites, and they no longer raised their heads. The land was at rest for forty years in the days of Gideon.
Jerubbaal son of Joash went and lived in his own house.
Gideon had seventy sons born from his own body, for he had many wives.
His concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.
Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash, in Ophrah of Ezri’s father.
After Gideon died, the Israelites turned back and prostituted themselves by following the Baals. They made a covenant with Baal-berith to be their god.
The Israelites did not remember the Lord their God, who had rescued them from all their enemies around them.
They showed no kindness to the household of Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, in return for all the good he had done for Israel.
Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem, to his mother’s brothers, and spoke with them and with the whole clan of his mother’s father’s household, saying:

“Speak in the hearing of all the men of Shechem: ‘Which is better for you: that seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, should rule over you, or that one man should rule over you?’ Remember that I am your bone and your flesh.”
His mother’s brothers spoke all these words about him in the hearing of all the men of Shechem. Their hearts inclined toward Abimelech, for they said, “He is our brother.”
And they gave him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith, the god of the covenant. With these Abimelech hired worthless and terrifying men, and they followed him.

And he entered his father's house at Ophrah and slaughtered his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on a single stone. But Jotham, Jerubbaal's youngest son, survived because he had hidden himself.
And all the men of Shechem and the whole house of Maalon gathered together. They went and made Abimelech king beside the oak of strife in Shechem.
And when Jotham was told, he went out and stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim. He raised his voice and cried out, saying to them, “Listen to me, men of Shechem, and may God listen to you.
The trees went out to anoint a king for themselves, and they said to the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’
And the olive tree said to them, ‘Should I leave my richness, for which God and people have honored me, and go to rule over the trees?’
And the trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come, reign over us.’
And the fig tree said to them, ‘Should I leave my sweetness and my good fruit and go to become ruler over the trees?’
And the trees said to the vine, ‘Come, reign over us.’
And the vine said to them, ‘Should I leave my wine and the joy of God and people and go to become ruler over the trees?’
And the trees said to the thornbush, ‘Come, reign over us.’

And the thornbush said to the trees, ‘If you truly anoint me to reign over you, come and take shelter under my shade. Otherwise, let fire come out of this thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’
And now, if you have acted truthfully and with integrity in making Abimelech king, and if that is how you have treated Jerubbaal and his household, and if you have treated him as his deeds deserved—
for my father fought on your behalf, risked his life, and saved you from the hands of Midian—

yet today you have risen against my father's household and slaughtered his sons, seventy men, on a single stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his servant woman, king over the men of Shechem because he is your brother.
If you have acted truthfully and with integrity toward Jerubbaal and his household this day, may you be blessed and rejoice in Abimelech, and may he also rejoice in you.
But if not, let fire come out of Abimelech and consume the men of Shechem and the house of Maalon. And if not, let fire come out of the men of Shechem and the house of Maalon and consume Abimelech.”
And Jotham fled and escaped, and went along the road to Beer. He lived there to keep away from his brother Abimelech.
And Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years.
And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and the men of Shechem despised the house of Abimelech,

to bring upon him the wrongdoing committed against Jerubbaal's seventy sons, and to bring their blood upon their brother Abimelech, who slaughtered them, and upon the men of Shechem, because they strengthened his hands to slaughter his brothers.
And the men of Shechem set an ambush for him on the mountaintops, and they robbed everyone who passed by them along the road. And Abimelech was told.
And Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers came and entered Shechem, and the men of Shechem put their trust in him.
And they went out into the fields, gathered the grapes from their vineyards, trod the winepresses, and held dances. They entered the temple of their god, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech.

And Gaal son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is the son of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his servant his governor, together with the men of Hamor, Shechem’s father? And why should we serve him?”
“If only this people were in my hands! I would remove Abimelech and say to Abimelech, ‘Increase your army and come out against me!’”
And Zebul, the ruler of the city, heard the words of Gaal son of Ebed and became furious.
He sent messengers with gifts to Abimelech, saying, “Look, Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem, and they are besieging the city against you.
Now rise during the night, you and the army with you, and lie in ambush in the fields.
In the morning, as the sun rises, get up early and advance against the city. He and the army with him will come out against you, and you shall do to him whatever your hand finds possible.”
And Abimelech and the whole army with him rose during the night and lay in ambush around Shechem in four companies.
In the morning Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the entrance to the city gate, and Abimelech and the whole army with him rose from their ambush.

And Gaal son of Ebed saw the army and said to Zebul, “Look, an army is coming down from the mountaintops.” And Zebul said to him, “You are seeing the shadows of the mountains as though they were men.”
And Gaal spoke again and said, “Look, an army is coming down from the seaward side, by the center of the land, and one company is coming along the road of the oak of the watchmen.”
And Zebul said to him, “Where is your mouth now, which said, ‘Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?’ Is that not the army you despised? Now go out and fight against him!”
And Gaal went out at the head of the men of Shechem and fought against Abimelech.
And Abimelech pursued him, and he fled before him. Many fell wounded, all the way to the city gates.
Abimelech stayed at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his brothers so that they could no longer live in Shechem.
On the following day the people went out into the fields, and Abimelech was told.
He took the army, divided it into three companies, and lay in ambush with it. He looked, and there was an army coming out of the city. He rose against them and struck them down.
And Abimelech and the companies with him formed their battle line and took their stand at the city gate, while the two companies spread out against everyone in the fields and struck them down.
And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. They captured the city, slaughtered the people in it, demolished the city, and desecrated it.
And all the men of the tower of Shechem heard and went into the stronghold of the temple of Bethel-berith.
And Abimelech was told that all the men of the tower of Shechem had gathered together.

And Abimelech went up Mount Zalmon, he and the whole army with him. Abimelech took an axe in his hand, cut a load of wood, took it, and put it on his shoulders. He said to his army, “What you see me doing, hurry and do yourselves, just as I do.”

And each of them also cut a load of wood. They lifted their loads, followed Abimelech, and placed them against the stronghold. They burned the stronghold over those inside it, and all the people of the tower of Shechem died, about a thousand men and women.
And Abimelech went to Thebez, encamped around it, and captured it.
There was a strong tower in the middle of the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled there. They shut themselves in and went up onto the roof of the tower.
And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it, and Abimelech approached the door of the tower.
And a woman threw a piece of a millstone onto his head and crushed Abimelech’s skull.
He quickly called out to his young armor-bearer and said to him, “Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say, ‘A woman killed him.’” His young attendant thrust him through, and Abimelech died.
When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, each man went back to his own place.
And God brought back upon Abimelech’s own head the evil he had done to his father by killing his seventy brothers.
And God brought all the evil of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads, and the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them.
After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, the son of his uncle, a man of Issachar, arose to save Israel. He lived in Samaria, in the hill country of Ephraim.
He judged Israel for twenty-three years, and he died and was buried in Samaria.
After him, Jair the Gileadite arose and judged Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty-two sons who rode thirty-two donkeys, and they had thirty-two towns. He called them the villages of Jair, as they are called to this day; they are in Gilead.
And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

The Israelites again did evil before the Lord. They worshiped the Baals and Ashtaroth, the gods of the Syrians, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. They abandoned the Lord and did not serve him.
The Lord’s anger burned against Israel, and he handed them over to the Philistines and the Ammonites.
At that time they shattered and crushed the Israelites for eighteen years—all the Israelites beyond the Jordan, in the land of the Amorites in Gilead.
The Ammonites crossed the Jordan to wage war against Judah, Benjamin, and the house of Ephraim, and the Israelites were greatly distressed.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord and said, “We have sinned against you, for we have abandoned our God and worshiped the Baals.”
And the Lord said to the Israelites, “Did not the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, Moab, and the Philistines
and the Sidonians, Amalek, and Canaan oppress you? You cried out to me, and I saved you from their hands.
But you abandoned me and served foreign gods. Therefore I will no longer save you.
Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen for yourselves, and let them save you in the time of your distress.”
And the Israelites said to the Lord, “We have sinned. Do to us whatever seems pleasing to you, but, Lord, only save us this day.”
They removed the foreign gods from among them and worshiped the Lord alone. But he was not reconciled with the people, and his spirit became [?] because of Israel’s suffering.
The Ammonites went out and camped in Gilead, and the Israelites went out and camped at the watchtower.
The leaders of the people of Gilead said to one another, “The man who begins to fight against the Ammonites shall become the head of all the inhabitants of Gilead.”
Jephthah the Gileadite was a man of great strength, and he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead fathered Jephthah.
Gilead’s wife bore him sons. When his wife’s sons grew up, they drove Jephthah away and said to him, “You shall not inherit anything in our father’s house, for you are the son of a prostitute.”
Jephthah fled from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob. Worthless men gathered around Jephthah and went out with him.
After some time, the Ammonites went to war against the Israelites.
When the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah back from the land of Tob.
They said to Jephthah, “Come and be our commander, and let us fight against the Ammonites.”
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “Did you not hate me, drive me out of my father’s house, and send me away from you? Why have you now come to me when you are in distress?”

The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “It is not so. Rather, we have come to you so that you may go with us, and we may fight against the Ammonites, and you may be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.”
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “If you bring me back to fight against the Ammonites, and the Lord delivers them into my power, shall I be ruler?”
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “Let the Lord be a witness between us if we do not act according to your word.”
Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people appointed him as their head and leader. Jephthah spoke all his words before the Lord at Mizpah.
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, saying, “What is there between you and me that you have come against me to fight in my land?”

The king of the Ammonites said to Jephthah’s messengers, “Why did Israel take my land when it came up from Egypt, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and as far as the Jordan? Now return it to me peacefully, and I will go away.” The messengers returned to Jephthah.
Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites.
He said to him, “Thus say Israel and Jephthah: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites when they came out of Egypt.”
But Israel traveled through the wilderness as far as the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.

Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, “Let me pass through your land.” But the king of Edom would not listen. Israel also sent to the king of Moab, but he was unwilling, and Israel remained at Kadesh.

Israel traveled through the wilderness, went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab, came to the eastern side of the land of Moab, and camped beyond the Arnon. They did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was Moab’s boundary.
Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon and of the Amorites. Israel said to him, “Let me pass through your land to my own place.”
Sihon was unwilling to let Israel pass through his territory. Sihon gathered all his people, camped at Jahaz, and fought against Israel.
The Lord, the God of Israel, delivered Sihon and all his people into Israel’s hands. Israel struck them down and took possession of the land of the Amorites who lived in that land.
Israel took possession of all the territory of the Amorites, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
Now the Lord, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites before his people Israel. Will you take possession of their land?
Will you not possess whatever Chemosh your god has given you to possess? And whatever the Lord our God has given us to possess before you, we will possess.
Now, are you any better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend with Israel or wage war against them?

While Israel lived in Heshbon and its surrounding towns, in Aroer and its surrounding towns, and in all the cities along the bank of the Jordan for three hundred years, why did they not recover them during that time?
I have done you no wrong, but you are doing me harm by making war against me. May the Lord, who is to judge, judge today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.
The king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words that Jephthah sent him.
The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh and through the lookout post of Gilead, and from the lookout post of Gilead he crossed over to the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to the Lord and said, “If you will indeed deliver the Ammonites into my hands—”
And whoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites, I will offer that person to the Lord as a burnt offering.
Then Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the Lord delivered them into his hands.
He struck them down from Aroer as far as the approach to Minnith—twenty cities—and as far as Abel of the vineyards, inflicting a very great defeat. The Ammonites were subdued before the Israelites.
Jephthah came to his house at Mizpah, and there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. She was his beloved only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter.

When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, “Alas, my daughter! You have brought me low; you have become an obstacle to me, for I have opened my mouth to the Lord concerning you, and I cannot take it back.”
She said to him, “If you have opened your mouth to the Lord concerning me, do to me what you have spoken, since the Lord has avenged you on your enemies, the Ammonites.”
She said to her father, “Do this for me: leave me alone for two months, so that I and my companions may go and wander through the mountains and mourn my virginity.”
He said to her, “Go.” He sent her away for two months, and she and her companions went and mourned her virginity in the mountains.
At the end of the two months she returned to her father, and he fulfilled the vow he had made concerning her. She had never known a man.
It became a custom in Israel to mourn Jephthah’s daughter. Year after year, the daughters of Israel gathered to mourn the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite for four days each year.
The men of Ephraim gathered and came to Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, “Why did you go to fight against the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? Now we will burn your house down over you.”
Jephthah said to them, “My people and I were oppressed, and the Ammonites afflicted me severely. I appealed to you, but you did not save me from their hands.

When I saw that there was no one to save me, I took my life in my hands and crossed over to the Ammonites, and the Lord delivered them into my hands. Why, then, have you come to me today to fight against me?”

Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck down Ephraim, because the survivors of Ephraim had said, “You Gileadites are in the midst of Ephraim and in the midst of Manasseh.”

Gilead seized the fords of the Jordan belonging to Ephraim. Whenever the survivors of Ephraim said, “Let us cross over,” the men of Gilead said to them, “Are you also from Ephraim?” They answered, “We are not from among them.”

They said to them, “Give us a sign and say, ‘Ear of grain, ear of grain.’” They could not pronounce it that way, so they seized them and slaughtered them at the fords of the Jordan. At that time forty-two thousand men of Ephraim fell.
Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his own city in Gilead.
After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.
He had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He gave his daughters in marriage outside his family and brought in thirty wives from outside for his sons. He judged Israel for seven years.
Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.
After him, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel for ten years.
Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.
After him, Abdon son of Hillel, the Pirathonite, judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode seventy donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years.
Abdon son of Hillel, the Pirathonite, died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of Amalek.
The Israelites again did evil before the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.
There was a man from Zorah, of the tribe of Dan, whose name was Manoah. His wife was barren and had borne no children.
The angel of the Lord appeared to the woman and said to her, “Look, you are barren and have not given birth, but you will conceive and bear a son.”
Now be careful not to drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean.

For you will conceive and bear a son. No iron blade is to touch his head, for the child will be a Nazirite dedicated to God from the womb, and he will begin to deliver Israel from the hands of the Philistines.

The woman went in and said to her husband, “A man of God came to me. His appearance was like the appearance of an angel of God, very awe-inspiring. I asked him, ‘Where are you from?’ But he did not tell me his name.”

“He said to me, ‘You will conceive and bear a son. Now do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean, for the child will be a Nazirite dedicated to God from his mother’s womb until the day of his death.’”
Manoah pleaded with the Lord and said, “O Lord, let the man of God whom you sent to us come to us again and teach us what we should do for the child who is to be born.”
God heard Manoah’s voice, and the angel of God came again to his wife while she was sitting in the field. Manoah her husband was not with her.
The woman hurried and ran to tell her husband. She said to him, “The man who came to me that day has appeared to me!”
Manoah got up and followed his wife. He came to the man and said to him, “Are you the man who spoke to my wife?” The angel said, “I am.”
Manoah said, “Now, when your words come true, what rules should govern the child’s life, and what should he do?”
The angel said to Manoah, “She must be careful about everything I told your wife.
She must not eat anything that comes from the vine, drink wine or strong drink, or eat anything unclean. She must carefully observe everything I commanded her.”
Manoah said to the angel, “Let us persuade you to stay, and prepare a young goat for you.”

The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “Even if you persuade me to stay, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the Lord.” For Manoah did not know that he was an angel of the Lord.
Manoah said to the angel of the Lord, “What is your name, so that when your words come true, we may honor you?”
The angel of the Lord said to him, “Why do you ask about my name? It is wonderful.”
Manoah took the young goat and the offering and offered them on the rock to the Lord, who works wonders. Manoah and his wife watched.
As the flame rose from the altar toward heaven, the angel of the Lord ascended in the flame of the altar. Manoah and his wife watched, and they fell facedown on the ground.
The angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah or his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was an angel of the Lord.
Manoah said to his wife, “We will certainly die, because we have seen God.”

His wife said to him, “If the Lord had wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted the burnt offering and the offering from our hands. Nor would he have revealed all these things to us from time to time, or let us hear these things.”
The woman bore a son and named him Samson. The child grew, and the Lord blessed him.
The Spirit of the Lord began to move within him in the camp of Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah and saw a woman there among the daughters of the Philistines, and she pleased him.
He went up and told his father and mother, saying, “I saw a woman in Timnah among the daughters of the Philistines. Now get her for me as a wife.”

His father and mother said to him, “Is there no woman among the daughters of your kinsmen or among all my people, that you must go and take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?” Samson said to his father, “Get her for me, for she is pleasing to my eyes.”
His father and mother did not know that this was from the Lord, for he was seeking retribution against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. Samson turned aside into the vineyards of Timnah, and suddenly a young lion roared at him.
The Spirit of the Lord came powerfully upon him, and he tore the lion apart as though it were a young goat, although he had nothing in his hand. He did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
They went down and spoke with the woman, and she seemed pleasing to Samson.
After some days he returned to take her as his wife, and he turned aside to look at the lion’s carcass. There was a swarm of bees in the lion’s mouth, and honey.
He took it into his mouth and ate as he walked along. He went to his father and mother and gave them some, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had taken the honey out of the lion’s mouth.
His father went down to the woman, and Samson held a wedding feast there for seven days, for that was what young men customarily did.
When they became afraid of him, they assigned thirty companions to him, and these stayed with him.

Samson said to them, “I will put a riddle to you. If you can solve it for me during the seven days of this feast and discover its meaning, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothing.
But if you cannot solve it for me, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothing.” They said to him, “Tell us your riddle, and we will listen to it.”
He said to them, “Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came sweetness.” For three days they could not solve his riddle.
On the fourth day they said to Samson’s wife, “Entice your husband to tell you the riddle, or we will burn you and your father’s house. Did you invite us here to impoverish us?”

Samson’s wife wept before him and said to him, “You hate me and do not love me, for you have not told me the riddle you put to the men of my people.” Samson said to her, “Look, I have not told my father or mother. Should I now tell you?”
She wept before him throughout the seven days of the feast. On the seventh day he told her, because she kept pleading with him, and she told the men of her people.

On the seventh day, before sunset, the men of the city said to him, “What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?” Samson said to them, “If you had not subdued my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle.”

The Spirit of the Lord came powerfully upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and killed thirty men there. He took their clothing and gave it to those who had solved the riddle. Samson was furious with anger and went up to his father’s house.
Samson’s wife married his best man, who had been his companion.
After some days, during the wheat harvest, Samson visited his wife, bringing a young goat. He said, “I will go into the room to my wife.” But her father would not let him go in to her.
Her father said, “I was certain that you hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister better than she is? Let her be yours instead.”
Samson said, “This time I will be blameless toward the Philistines if I do them harm.”
Samson went and caught three hundred foxes. He took torches and tied the foxes to one another, tail to tail. He placed a torch between each pair of tails and tied the torches in the middle.

And he set fire to the torches and released them into the Philistines’ fields. He burned the harvest and what had already been reaped, from the stacks to the standing grain, and even the vineyards and olive trees.

The Philistines said, “Who did this?” And they said, “Samson, the Timnite’s son-in-law, because he took Samson’s wife away and gave her to his companion.” Then the Philistines went up and burned her father’s house, the woman, and her father with fire.
Samson said to them, “Even if you do as much again, I will still not be satisfied, but will exact my revenge from each one of you.”
He struck them from shin to thigh with very great blows. Then he went down and lived beside the ravine, in the cave of Etam.
The Philistines went up and encamped in Judah and spread out around Lehi.
A man of Judah said to them, “Why have you come up against me?” The Philistines said, “We have come up to bind Samson and do to him as he did to us.”

Three thousand men of Judah went down to the edge of the rock of Etam and said to Samson, “Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why have you done this to us?” Samson said to them, “As they did to me, so I did to them.”

They said to him, “We have come down to bind you and hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson said to them, “Swear to me that you yourselves will not kill me. Hand me over to them, but never attack me yourselves.”
They swore to him and said, “No, we will only bind you and hand you over to them, but we will certainly not kill you.” They bound him with three new ropes and brought him up from the rock.

He came to Jawbone, and the Philistines shouted and ran toward him. The Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him, and the ropes on his arms became like tow when it catches fire, and the bonds melted away from his arms.
He found a donkey’s jawbone lying there, reached out his hand, took it, and struck down a thousand men with it.
Samson said, “With a donkey’s jawbone I will utterly wipe them out, for with a donkey’s jawbone I killed a thousand men.”
When he finished speaking, he threw the jawbone from his hand and named the place “Slaughter of the Jawbone.”

He became very thirsty and cried out to the Lord, saying, “You have brought about this great deliverance through the hand of your servant. And now shall we die of thirst, and shall I fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”
The Lord opened a hollow in the jawbone, and water came out of it. He drank, his spirit returned to him, and he was refreshed. Therefore he named it “The Spring Called Jawbone,” as it is to this day.
He judged Israel in the days of the Philistines for twenty years.
Samson went from there to Gaza, saw a prostitute there, and went in to her.

The people of Gaza were informed and said, “Samson has come here.” They surrounded him and lay in wait for him all night at the city gate. They remained silent all night and said, “Let us stay here until morning, and we will kill him.”

Samson slept until midnight. At midnight he arose, tore loose the city gates with their thresholds, lifted them together with their bars, and put them on his shoulders. He carried them up to the top of the mountain opposite Hebron and set them down there.
After this he fell in love with a woman beside the ravine of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.

The rulers of the Philistines went up to her and said, “Deceive him and find out what gives him his great strength, and how we can find a way to overcome him and bind him to make him weak. Each of us will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver.”
Delilah said to Samson, “Tell me what gives you your great strength, and how you could be bound to make you weak.”
Samson said to her, “If they bind me with seven fresh sinews that have not dried, I will become weak and be like any other man.”
The rulers of the Philistines brought her seven fresh, undried sinews, and she bound him with them.

Men were lying in ambush for him in the storeroom. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He snapped the sinews as a cord of tow snaps when exposed to fire, and his strength remained undiscovered.
Delilah said to Samson, “Look, you have deceived me and told me lies. Now at least tell me what you can be bound with.”
He said to her, “If they bind me securely with seven new ropes that have never been used for any work, I will become weak and be like any other man.”

Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” Men were lying in ambush for him in the storeroom, but he snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.

Delilah said to Samson, “How long will you deceive me and tell me lies? Now tell me what you can be bound with.” He said to her, “If you weave the seven locks of my hair into the warp and fasten them to the wall with pegs, I will become weak like any other man.”

Delilah put him to sleep, took the seven locks of his hair together with the warp, and fastened them to the wall with pegs. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He awoke from his sleep and pulled the pegs, together with the woven cloth and the warp, out of the wall, and his strength remained undiscovered.
Delilah said to him, “How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not sincere toward me? You have deceived me these three times and have not told me what gives you your great strength.”
And when she pressured him with her words all night long, pestering him and wearing him out to the point of death,

he told her everything in his heart. He said to her, “No razor shall touch my head, because I have been a Nazirite of God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become weak and be like all other people.”

When Delilah saw that he had told her everything in his heart, she sent for the rulers of the Philistines and said, “Come up this time, for he has told me everything in his heart.” All the rulers of the Philistines came up to her, bringing the silver in their hands.
She put him to sleep in her lap, called a barber, and shaved off the seven locks of his hair. He began to weaken, and his strength left him.
Delilah said, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He awoke from his sleep and said, “I will go out and do as I always have, and shake myself free.” But he did not know that the Lord had left him.
The Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza. They bound him with iron shackles, and he ground grain in the prison.
The hair on his head began to grow after it had been shaved off.
The rulers of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to celebrate. They said, “Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hands.”
When the people saw him, they praised their god, saying, “Our god has delivered our enemy into our hands, the destroyer of our land, who multiplied the number of our wounded.”

When their hearts were merry, they said, “Call Samson out of the prison, and let him entertain us.” They called Samson out of the prison and made sport of him, and they placed him between the two pillars.
Samson said to the boy who was holding his hand, “Let me feel the pillars on which this building rests, so that I can lean against them.”
The building was full of men and women, and all the rulers of the Philistines were there. On the roof were about three thousand men and women watching Samson’s performance.
Samson cried out to the Lord and said, “Lord, Lord of hosts, remember me and strengthen me just this once more, O God, so that I may take revenge on these Philistines for my two eyes.”
Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested and leaned against them, against one with his right hand and against the other with his left.

Samson said, “Let me die with these Philistines.” He pushed with his strength, and the house fell on all the rulers and on all the people gathered inside it. Those Samson killed at his death were more numerous than those he killed during his life.

His brothers and his father’s entire household came down, picked him up, brought him away, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol, in the tomb of his father Manoah. He had judged Israel for twenty years.
There was a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah.

He said to his mother, “The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse and spoke in my hearing—the silver is with me; I took it.” His mother said, “May you be blessed by the Lord, my son.”

He returned the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother, and his mother said, “I have solemnly dedicated the silver from my hand to the Lord and set it apart to make a carved image and a cast image. Now I will return it to you.”

He returned the silver to his mother, and his mother took two hundred pieces of silver and gave them to the metalworker. He made them into a carved image and a cast image, and they were in Micah’s house.
Micah’s house was a house of God for him. He made an ephod and teraphim and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.
In those days there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was pleasing in his own eyes.
There was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah, from the clan of Judah. He was a Levite and lived there.
The man left the town of Bethlehem in Judah to live wherever he could find a place. As he traveled, he came to the hill country of Ephraim and to Micah’s house.
Micah said to him, “Where do you come from?” He said to him, “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to live wherever I can find a place.”
Micah said to him, “Stay here with me and be a father and a priest to me. I will give you ten pieces of silver each year, a set of clothes, and food to live on.” So the Levite went with him.
He began to live with the man, and the young man became like one of his sons.
Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in Micah’s house.
Micah said, “Now I know that the Lord has done good to me, because the Levite has become my priest.”

In those days there was no king in Israel. In those days the tribe of Dan was seeking an inheritance for itself to live in, because up to that time no inheritance had fallen to it among the tribes of Israel.

The Danites sent five men from their clans, men representing their tribe, mighty men from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and explore it. They said to them, “Go and examine the land.” They went to the hill country of Ephraim, as far as Micah’s house, and lodged there.
While they were in Micah’s house, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. They turned aside there and said to him, “Who brought you here? What are you doing here? What do you have here?”
He said to them, “Micah has done such and such for me. He hired me, and I became his priest.”
They said to him, “Please inquire of God, so that we may know whether the journey we are making will succeed.”
The priest said to them, “Go in peace. The journey you are making is before the Lord.”

The five men went to Laish and saw the people there, who lived securely, like the Sidonians, quiet and confident. No one could say a word to anyone in the land [?] the heir of the treasures. They were far from Sidon and had no dealings with the Syrians.
The five men came to their brothers in Zorah and Eshtaol, and their brothers said to them, “Why are you sitting here?”

They said, “Come, let us go up against them! We entered and traveled through the land as far as Laish, and we saw the people living there securely, like the Sidonians. They are far from Sidon and have no dealings with the Syrians. Come, let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and it is very good. Are you just sitting still? Why are you now holding back from going in and taking possession of the land?”
“When you go, you will find a complacent people and a spacious land, for God has given it into our hands—a place lacking nothing that is found on earth.”
Six hundred men from the clans of the tribe of Dan set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, equipped with weapons for battle.
They went up and camped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. That is why that place is called the Camp of Dan to this day. It is behind Kiriath-jearim.
They went on from there, came to the hill country of Ephraim, and reached Micah’s house.

The five men who had gone to scout out the land of Laish spoke to their brothers and said, “Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a cast image? Now consider what you should do.”
They turned aside there and entered the house of the young Levite, which was in Micah’s household, and asked about his well-being.
The six hundred men from the tribe of Dan stood at the entrance to the gate, equipped with their weapons for battle.

The five men who had gone to scout out the land went up, rushed in, and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the cast image. The priest stood at the entrance to the gate with the six hundred men equipped with weapons for battle.
They entered Micah’s house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the cast image. The priest said to them, “What are you doing?”

They said to him, “Be quiet! Put your hand over your mouth. Come with us and be a father and a priest to us. Is it better for you to be priest to one man’s household than to be priest to a tribe and a clan of Israel?”
The priest’s heart was glad. He took the ephod, the household gods, the carved image, and the cast image, and went into the midst of the company.
They turned and went on, driving the whole household and its valuable possessions ahead of them.
When they had gone some distance from Micah’s house, Micah and the men who were in his houses raised an outcry together and caught up with the people of Dan.
The people of Dan turned around and said to Micah, “What is the matter with you? Why are you shouting?”
Micah said, “You have taken the gods I made for myself, along with the priest, and gone away. What do I have left now? How can you say to me, ‘Why are you shouting?’”
The people of Dan said to him, “Do not let your voice be heard behind us, or men embittered in spirit may attack you and take your life and the lives of your household.”
The people of Dan went on their way. When Micah saw that they were stronger than he was, he returned to his house.
They took what Micah had made and his priest, and went to Laish, to a people who were quiet and confidently secure. They struck them down with the sword and burned the city.
There was no one to rescue them, because they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone. It lay in the valley of Beth-rehob. They rebuilt the city and lived in it.
They named it Dan after their ancestor Dan, who was born to Israel. The city's former name was Laish.
The descendants of Dan set up Micah's carved image for themselves. Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Manasseh, and his sons were priests for the tribe of Dan until the day the land went into captivity.
They kept the carved image that Micah had made set up for themselves throughout the time that the house of God was in Shiloh.
In those days there was no king in Israel. A Levite was living as a stranger in the region of the hill country of Ephraim, and he took a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
His concubine became angry with him and left him for her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah. She stayed there for three months.

The man got up and went after her to speak tenderly to her, reconcile her to himself, and bring her back to him. His servant was with him, along with a pair of donkeys. They went to her father’s house. When the girl’s father saw him, he came out to meet him.
His father-in-law, the girl's father, brought him inside, and he stayed with him for three days. They ate, drank, and slept there.
