On the fourth day they rose early in the morning, and he got up to leave. The girl's father said to his son-in-law, “Strengthen yourself with a piece of bread, and then you may go.”
The two of them sat down and ate and drank together. The girl’s father said to his son-in-law, “Now settle in here for the night, and let your heart be glad.”
The man got up to leave, but his father-in-law pressed him to stay, so he stayed and spent another night there.
On the fifth day he rose early in the morning to leave. The girl's father said, “Strengthen yourself with bread, and rest until the day draws to a close.” So the two of them ate and drank.

The man got up to leave with his concubine and his young servant. The girl's father said to him, “Look, the day has turned toward evening. Spend the night here and let your heart be cheerful. Tomorrow you can rise early for your journey and go home.”
But the man was unwilling to stay there overnight. He got up and left, and came to a place opposite Jebus, that is, Jerusalem. With him were a pair of saddled donkeys, and his concubine was with him.
They were opposite Jebus, and the day was far spent. The servant said to his master, “Come, let us turn aside into the city of the Jebusites and spend the night there.”
His master said to him, “We will not turn aside into this city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites. Instead, let us go on to Gibeah.”
He said to his young servant, “Come, let us approach one of these places and spend the night there, either in Gibeah or in Ramah.”
They continued on their way, and the sun set as they neared Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They turned aside there to enter Gibeah and spend the night. He went in and sat in the city square, but no one took them into his house to spend the night.
Then an old man came in late from his work in the field. The man was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living as a stranger in Gibeah. The men of that place were descendants of Benjamin.
He looked up and saw the traveler in the city square. The old man said, “Where are you going, and where have you come from?”

He said to him, “We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the region of the hill country of Ephraim, because I am from there. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to my father's house. But there is no one to take us into his house.
There is straw and fodder for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me, your maidservant, and your young servant. Your servants lack nothing.”
The old man said, “Peace be with you. I will provide whatever you need. Only do not spend the night in the square.”
He brought him into his house and gave the donkeys fodder. They washed their feet, ate, and drank.

While their hearts were cheerful, men of the city, wicked men, surrounded the house and pounded on the door. They spoke to the old man, the owner of the house, saying, “Bring out the man who entered your house, so that we may have sex with him.”
The owner of the house went out to them and said, “No, my brothers! Do not act wickedly. Since this man has entered my house, do not commit this outrage.”
“Here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. I will bring them outside, and you may violate them and do to them whatever pleases you. But do not do this disgraceful thing to this man.”
But the men would not listen. So the man took his concubine and brought her outside to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning, and let her go at dawn.
The woman came back in the morning and fell at the threshold of the door of the man's house, where her master was, and breathed her last.
Her master rose in the morning, opened the doors of the house, and went out to go on his way. And there was his concubine, lying at the door with her hand on the threshold.
He said to her, “Get up, and let us go.” But she gave him no answer, for she was dead. He lifted her onto the donkey, and the man got up and went to his own home.
When he entered his house, he took a sword, seized his concubine, and cut her up along her bones into twelve pieces. He sent them throughout all the tribes of Israel.
Everyone who saw it said, “Nothing like this has happened or been seen since the day the Israelites came out of the land of the Egyptians until today. Now consider this, take counsel, and speak.”
All the Israelites came out, and the people assembled as one man, from Dan to Beersheba, together with the land of Gilead, before the Lord at Mizpah.
The leaders of all the people and all the tribes of Israel took their places in the whole assembly of the people of God: four hundred thousand men with drawn swords.
The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah. The Israelites said, “Tell us where this evil took place.”
The Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, answered, “My concubine and I came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night.
The men of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house where I was during the night. They wanted to kill me, and they abused my concubine and strangled her, and she died.
I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent her throughout all the territory of Israel’s inheritance, because they committed great harm and an outrage in Israel.
And here we are, all Israelites. Give us an answer and advice.”
All the people rose as one man and said, “None of us will go under his own roof, and none of us will turn aside to his own house.
Now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot.”

“But let us take ten men out of every hundred from all the tribes of Israel, a hundred out of every thousand, and a thousand out of every ten thousand, to obtain provisions for the whole army going to Gibeah of Benjamin because of all the disgraceful things they did in Israel.”
All Israel assembled as one man, coming from the cities.
The tribes of Israel sent men throughout the whole tribe of Benjamin and said, “What is this evil that has taken place among you?
Now look to the wicked men of Gibeah, the sons of Belial, and let us kill them and remove the evil from Israel.” But the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their brothers, the Israelites.
The Benjaminites gathered from their cities at Gibeah to go out to war against the Israelites.
On that day the Benjaminites mustered twenty-five thousand men with drawn swords from their various cities, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, of whom seven hundred men were mustered.
These were chosen young men from all the people, skilled with both hands. All of them were slingers who could sling stones at a hair without missing.
All the men of Israel, apart from the Benjaminites, passed in review: four hundred thousand men who drew the sword, all of them warriors.
They rose and went up to Bethel and inquired of God. The Israelites said, “Who shall go first for us to fight against the Benjaminites?” The Lord said, “Judah shall go first.”
The Israelites rose in the morning and camped at Gibeah.
The men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin, and the men of Israel drew up their battle lines against them at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of the city and killed twenty-two thousand men of Israel that day, laying them low on the ground.
The men of Israel strengthened themselves again and once more drew up their battle lines in the place where they had drawn them up on the first day.
The Israelites went up and wept before the Lord until evening. They inquired of the Lord and said, “Shall we again go to battle against Benjamin our brother?” The Lord said, “Go up against them.”
And the Israelites went out to battle against the Benjaminites on the second day.
And Benjamin went out against them in battle on the second day and again struck down eight thousand men from the people, all of them swordsmen.
And all the Israelites and all the people went up and came to Bethel. They sat and wept before the Lord, fasted that day, and offered burnt offerings of well-being before the Lord.
For the ark of the covenant of the Lord God was there in those days, and Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, stood before it in those days.

And the Israelites asked the Lord, saying, “Shall we again go out to battle against the descendants of Benjamin, our brother, or shall we stop?” And the Lord said, “Go out, and tomorrow I will deliver him into your hands.”
And the Israelites stationed men in ambush around Gibeah.
And the Israelites went out against Benjamin on the third day and drew up their battle lines against Gibeah as they had the first and second times.

And the Benjaminites went out against the people and were drawn away from the city. They began to inflict casualties among the people as they had the first and second times, along the roads, one of which went up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah. There in the open country they struck down about thirty men of Israel.
And the Benjaminites said, “They are being slaughtered before us as they were the first time.” But the Israelites said, “Let us flee and draw them away from the city onto the roads.”
And all the men of Israel rose, each from his own position, and drew up their battle lines at Baal-tamar. The Israelites lying in ambush fought from their position west of Gibeah.
And ten thousand chosen men from all Israel came opposite Gibeah, and the battle grew fierce. But the Benjaminites did not know that disaster had come upon them.
The Lord defeated Benjamin before the Israelites, and that day the Israelites killed twenty-five thousand one hundred men of Benjamin, all of them men who drew the sword.
When the Benjaminites saw that they had been defeated, the men of Israel gave way to Benjamin, because they trusted in the men they had stationed in ambush around Gibeah.
And the men lying in ambush rushed forward and overran Gibeah. They entered and struck down the whole city with the edge of the sword.
And the men of Israel had agreed with those lying in ambush that they should use fire to send up a cloud of smoke from the city.

And the men of Israel turned away from the battle, and Benjamin began to inflict casualties among the Israelites lying in ambush, about thirty men, for they said, “They are surely being defeated before us, as in the first battle.”
And the signal rose thickly above the city like a pillar of smoke. Benjamin looked behind him, and behold, the destruction of the city was rising toward heaven.
And the men of Israel turned back, and the men of Benjamin were terrified, for they saw that disaster had come upon them.
And they fled from the men of Israel along the road to the wilderness, but the battle overtook them, and those coming out of the cities killed them in their midst.
And they struck down Benjamin and pursued him into Nua, as far as the place opposite Gibeah on the eastern side.
And eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them mighty warriors.

When the survivors saw this, they fled into the wilderness for refuge at the rock of Rimmon. The Israelites picked off five thousand of their men along the road and pressed the pursuit as far as Gilead, striking down two thousand men of Benjamin.
And all those of Benjamin who fell that day numbered twenty-five thousand swordsmen, all of them valiant men.
And the survivors escaped and fled into the wilderness for refuge at the rock of Rimmon, six hundred men. They remained at the rock of Rimmon for four months.

And the men of Israel turned back against the Benjaminites and struck them down with the edge of the sword, proceeding through the cities in turn, down to the livestock and everything found in every city. And the cities that had survived they [?] and burned with fire.
The men of Israel swore at Mizpah, saying, “None of us shall give his daughter to Benjamin as a wife.”
All the people came from Mizpah to Bethel and sat there before God until evening. They raised their voices and wept bitterly.
They said, “Why, Lord God of Israel, has this happened in Israel, that today one tribe should be completely destroyed from Israel?”
The next morning the people rose early, built an altar there, and offered burnt offerings of peace.

The Israelites said, “Who from all the tribes of Israel did not come up to this assembly before the Lord at Mizpah?” For a solemn oath had been taken concerning anyone who did not come up to Mizpah, saying, “He shall surely be put to death.”
The Israelites were consoled concerning Benjamin their brother, and said, “Today one tribe has been removed from Israel.”
“Now what shall we do for those who remain without wives? We have sworn by the Lord not to give them wives from among our daughters.”
They said, “Which one of the tribes of Israel did not come up before the Lord at Mizpah?” And indeed, no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp of the assembly.
The people were reviewed, and there was no man there from the house of Jabesh-gilead.
The people sent twelve thousand valiant men there and commanded them, saying, “Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword, including the women and the people.”
“This is what you shall do: devote to destruction every male and every woman who has shared a bed with a male.”

Among those of the house of Jabesh-gilead they found four hundred virgin girls who had not known a man by sharing a bed with a male. They brought them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.
The whole assembly sent word and spoke to the Benjaminites who were at the rock of Rimmon, inviting them to peace.
At that time Benjamin returned to the Israelites, and they gave them those wives who were among the women of Jabesh-gilead. This seemed satisfactory to them.
The people were comforted concerning Benjamin, for the Lord had made a breach among the tribes of Israel.
The elders of the people said, “What shall we do for the others who have no wives, since the women have been destroyed from Benjamin?”
They said, “An inheritance has been preserved for Benjamin, and the tribe must not be wiped out from Israel.”
“But we cannot give them wives from among our daughters, for we Israelites have sworn, saying, ‘Cursed be anyone who gives a wife to Benjamin.’”
They said, “Look, there is a recurring festival of the Lord at Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebanon, at Lebonah.”
They commanded the Benjaminites, saying, “Go and lie in ambush in the vineyards.”

“When you see the daughters of the inhabitants of Shiloh coming out to dance, come out of the vineyards, and let each man seize a wife for himself from among the daughters of Shiloh. Then go to the land of Benjamin.”

“When their fathers or brothers come to dispute with you, we shall say to them, ‘We showed them mercy, because not every man obtained his wife in the war, and you did not give them wives, so that you should incur any guilt.’”

The Benjaminites did so. They took wives according to their number from among the dancers whom they seized. They went away and returned, each to his own inheritance, rebuilt the cities, and lived in them.
At that time the Israelites departed, each to his own tribe and clan. They went out from there, each to his own inheritance.
In those days there was no king in Israel, and each man did what was pleasing in his own eyes.
